analysis.one_liner: Requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publicly disclose the names and claim details of people seeking compensation.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 19-9 vote in 2015 but never received a vote in the full House or Senate, and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that made products containing asbestos have paid out so many injury claims that many went bankrupt; as part of their bankruptcies, courts created trusts to compensate people who get sick from asbestos exposure. This bill would require those trusts to publish quarterly reports naming every person who files a claim, their exposure history, and the basis for any payment, and to share that information with defendants in ongoing asbestos lawsuits. Supporters called it transparency to prevent fraudulent or duplicate claims; opponents said it publicizes private medical information and helps companies contest legitimate claims. The bill passed the House Judiciary Committee but never received a vote in the full House or Senate, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing asbestos liability lawsuits gain the most. The bill gives them access to trust claim data they can use to challenge plaintiffs' cases, and the public reporting of claimant names helps them identify and dispute claims. Supporters argue this deters fraudulent claims, but the direct beneficiaries are the defendant corporations, not the people sickened by asbestos.

how_it_helps.text: It requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publish quarterly, on the public court docket, the name and exposure history of every claimant and the basis for each payment.

It obligates trusts, on written request, to hand over information about demands and payments to any party suing over asbestos liability — in practice, defense lawyers for companies facing asbestos suits.

analysis.who_pays: People with asbestos-related illnesses and their families. The public disclosure of claimant names and exposure histories could be used against them in court, the reporting burden would be paid out of trust funds set aside for victims, and the paperwork could slow payments to people who are often seriously ill and elderly.

drawbacks.text: The quarterly reports would publicly disclose each claimant's name and asbestos exposure history, information asbestos defendants could use to challenge victims' ongoing lawsuits, even though trusts were already audited and already reported aggregate data.

The reporting and on-demand disclosure duties would add administrative costs to trusts that are funded by fixed bankruptcy settlements, meaning money spent on compliance is money not available to pay asbestos victims — and the bill applied retroactively to trusts already operating.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — public transparency about how trusts pay claims — is legitimate in principle, but the design burdens the people the trusts exist to compensate: it publicizes claimants' names and exposure histories, which defendants can use to contest remaining lawsuits, and imposes reporting costs on trusts whose money belongs to future victims. It offers no corresponding benefit to sick workers or their families. Given that it never received a vote in either chamber, its practical effect was nil, but its design leaned toward the interests of asbestos defendants rather than claimants.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 19-9 and put it on the House calendar, but leadership never brought it up for a vote, and it died without ever reaching the House or Senate floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in January 2015, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and ordered reported by a 19-9 committee vote in May 2015.
The committee formally reported it on November 30, 2015, and placed it on the Union Calendar, which is the list of bills awaiting a floor vote.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 114th Congress: the House never voted on it, and it never received a Senate vote or a Senate companion's consideration, so it expired in January 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers are better off, because the disclosure regime they sought was never imposed — but neither did it pass, so no one's position actually changed.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote split 19-9 along party lines, with the Republican majority supporting the bill and the Democratic minority opposing it; it had only Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers
industries.note: The bill hands defendant companies a tool to contest remaining asbestos lawsuits by giving them on-demand access to trust claim data, and the stated rationale is preventing double recovery. Its practical benefit flows to firms facing asbestos liability, not to sick workers.
Lawyers representing asbestos claimants would face slower filings and clients whose claims are publicly identified and more easily challenged, though the bill does not bar any claim outright.

industries.industry: Asbestos bankruptcy trusts and their claimants
industries.note: Trusts exist to pay people sickened by asbestos; the bill imposes new reporting and disclosure duties on them that add cost and slow payments, with the burden ultimately falling on victims rather than the companies that created the trusts.
